sources.citation: Chirkova, Ekaterina 2007. Zai zhongyin yu shengdiao de lianxuti shang kan Shixingyu [Between stress and tone: tones in Shixing and other Qiangic languages]. Eastling / Dongfang yuyanxue 2: 143-152 (HAL hal-00162105v2).
sources.note: Guiqiong named only in lists: after Sun (2004:303) it is one of four Qiangic languages (Muya, Guiqiong, Namuyi, Shixing) where tone has a large distinctive role; then an areal conjecture that in the remaining Qiangic languages (Muya, Zhaba, Guiqiong, Ersu) the tone-bearing unit is not the syllable and affixes/particles lack independent tone, exemplified with Muya and Zhaba only. No Guiqiong-specific stress rule.

sources.citation: Chirkova, Katia 2022/2024. Vowel harmony in Sino-Tibetan languages (book chapter, HAL hal-03505376v2).
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Guiqiong vowel harmony after Rao 2015: 63-67; 'Monosyllabic verbs in Guiqiong have two tones: 35 and 55. The tone of the prefix shows some variation depending on the tone of the verb' (citing Rao 2015: 72-73, 83-86).

sources.citation: Chirkova, Katia 2020. Documenter la variation et le changement en contexte multilingue: le sud-ouest de la Chine. Memoire d'HDR, EHESS (HAL tel-04090419).
sources.note: Only describes Rao Min's thesis as covering 'sa phonologie (voyelles, consonnes, prosodie)'; no Guiqiong data on stress.

sources.citation: Chirkova, Katia 2020. Sino-Tibetan (handbook chapter 46, HAL hal-03090078v1).
sources.note: Nothing on stress; Guiqiong vowel inventory and vowel harmony (after Rao 2015: 63-67; Jiang 2015: 58-60) with tone-marked examples.

sources.citation: Gates, Jesse P. 2018. Review: A Grammar of Guiqiong: A Language of Sichuan (Jiang Li, Brill 2015). Asian Highlands Perspectives 51: 384-396.
sources.note: No stress statement. Second-hand report of Jiang 2015 ch.2: three tonemes correlated with onset type (voiceless=high, voiced=medial, breathy=low falling, p.54-56), a 'neutral tone.. very slight and short, similar to the neutral tone in Mandarin' (Jiang p.55), tone treated on pp.49-57, syllable p.58; notes Rao 2015 ch.3 (pp.69-111) treats tone in monosyllables, disyllables, affixes/clitics and sandhi.

sources.citation: Chirkova, Katia 2012. The Qiangic subgroup from an areal perspective: a case study of languages of Muli. Language and Linguistics 13.1: 133-170 (HAL hal-00553056v2).
sources.note: Guiqiong appears only in subgrouping lists; nothing on its prosody.

sources.citation: Thurgood, Graham & Randy LaPolla (eds.) 2003. The Sino-Tibetan Languages. London: Routledge (overview chapter, subgrouping).
sources.note: Guiqiong only in the Qiangic subgroup list (p.17) and index; no description.

sources.citation: Sun Hongkai 1990. Languages of the ethnic corridor in western Sichuan (transl. Jackson T.-S. Sun). Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 13.1: 1-31 [Guiqiong sketch sec. 1.5, pp. 11-12, Maiben commune, Yutong district, Kangding].
sources.note: Nothing on stress. States no consonant codas, no falling diphthongs, and 'A system of four tonemes exists, and is important for lexical differentiation.' (pp. 11-12).

sources.citation: Evans, Jonathan P. n.d. A Survey of Tibeto-Burman phonological phenomena (ms v10.2, Academia Sinica).
sources.note: Guiqiong listed only in segmental tables (prenasalized onsets, uvulars, apical vowels, after Sun et al. 1991); the survey has no stress section mentioning Guiqiong.

tone.says: Second-hand inventory (compiled from Sun et al. 1991 ZMYYC #17): four tones on the syllable ma -- 55 high level, 33 mid level, 35 high rising, 53 high falling -- with the note that the mid level tone is sometimes realized as low falling. No statement on sandhi, TBU or stress. (extracted text renders the tone numerals in a substituted font: the infinity glyph = 5, the pound glyph = 3; mapping verified on the Lahu entry of the same file, 45/54/33/21/11.).
